Copper: furnaces to rework at its US plant, German giant Aurubis warns profits will fall, shares drop more than 10%

Aurubis, Europe's largest copper producer, on Tuesday, November 24, forecast 2026/27 earnings below market expectations because of its recycling plant in Richmond, Georgia (United States), whose furnaces need to be modified. The shares fell as much as 13% [1][2][3][8].
The Hamburg-based group is targeting operating earnings before taxes of €430 million to €530 million for fiscal 2026/27, below market expectations, according to its regulatory statement [1].
The midpoint of the range, €480 million, is below the result for the fiscal year just ended: €516 million according to preliminary figures, compared with €355 million a year earlier [1][2].
The cause is Richmond: "certain components of the smelting furnaces need to be modified," Aurubis explains. Work on the furnaces' suspension system will take six months [1][2].
The plant will still weigh on earnings in 2026/27, roughly as much as last year, and will only reach full technical capacity in the second half of 2028 [1].
The shares were down 13% shortly before noon, then about 10%; basic resources were the worst sector in a slightly lower European Stoxx 600 index [2][3].
Key takeaway: Aurubis's American bet is costing more, and for longer, than planned, and this is the second piece of bad news about the plant in four months [1][5].

Richmond, near Augusta, cost about $800 million. It is designed to recycle up to 180,000 tons a year of complex recycling materials to recover copper, nickel, tin and precious metals [4]. In 2025, CEO Toralf Haag described it as the "pioneer of multimetal recycling in the United States" [4].
The target market is huge: US industry consumes about 1.8 million tons of copper a year and imports about half of what it processes, according to Aurubis [4].
In August, Aurubis had already delayed Richmond's ramp-up because of technical problems and a less favorable scrap mix, and cut the plant's medium-term earnings target [5][7].

Copper is everywhere: electrical wiring, electric cars, data centers. If your savings (life insurance, stock savings plan) include a European equity fund, Aurubis may be in it. Above all, this case is a reminder that building plants in the United States remains costly for European groups.

How it works: the "ad hoc" notice that sinks a stock

In Germany, a listed company must publish without delay, in an "ad hoc" statement, any information that could move its share price. That is what Aurubis did: its forecast of €430 million to €530 million was "below market expectations" [1], meaning below the average of analysts' forecasts, on which the share price was based. The gap is therefore corrected all at once, here with a drop of up to 13% [3]. For a smelter and recycler like Aurubis, earnings do not depend only on the copper price. They also depend on the fees it charges to process and refine ores and scrap, and Aurubis has already cited lower treatment charges as a drag [10]. A plant that runs poorly, like Richmond, drives up costs without earning those fees [1].
Precedents: Aurubis's warnings
August 31, 2023

Aurubis discovers a significant metal shortfall in its recycling business, abandons its earnings forecast of €450 million to €550 million, and its shares plunge as much as 18% [8]. The damage from this fraud, involving suppliers and employees, is later put at $198 million [9].
Recycling is a risky business: controlling what you buy and what you produce is tricky.
September 24, 2025
Aurubis starts production in Richmond, an investment of about $800 million and more than 240 jobs in Georgia [4].
It is the group's biggest bet outside Europe: its delays weigh heavily.
August 2026

Despite higher earnings and a forecast raised to €425 million to €525 million, the shares fall: Richmond's ramp-up is delayed [5][7]. Analyst Stefan Augustin of Warburg Research calls it a "disappointment" [6].
The market looks ahead: a good quarter does not make up for a delayed plant.

Canada: to speed up the Toronto-Quebec City high-speed rail line, Ottawa wants to expropriate without public hearings and hand land to a private consortium

Mark Carney's government wants to give the future Alto high-speed rail line, between Toronto and Quebec City, expropriation powers outside ordinary law: no public hearings, land transferred to the private consortium building the line, private arbitration for farmers. On Tuesday, November 24, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon defended a "nation-building project" [1][2][4].
The measures are contained in a 519-page ways and means motion, a prerequisite for the bill that is to implement the 2026 budget [1][2].
Alto would be exempt from the entire Expropriation Act, the Railway Relocation and Crossing Act, and key sections of the Railway Safety Act and the Impact Assessment Act [1].
Ottawa could expropriate without a public hearing and transfer ownership directly to the private consortium in charge of building the line, not just to the state [1][2].

For farms cut in two and municipal roads, disputes over crossings would go to private arbitration, with costs shared up to C$25,000 per party, on top of legal fees [1]. An owner could also be barred for four years from any construction or major work without the minister's permission [2].

Steven MacKinnon says these powers will save steps that could otherwise take years, without affecting procedural safeguards. He cites Montreal's REM light rail and Toronto's Ontario Line, which also have "tailored regimes" for acquiring land [2][3].

Conservative MP Michael Barrett denounces a separate regime that replaces the Expropriation Act, and worries about the cost and disruption in rural eastern Ontario and Quebec [2]. The Conservatives and the Bloc Québécois oppose the plan; the NDP supports it but has doubts about these powers [1].
Key takeaway: Ottawa wants to clear legal obstacles before buying land for the high-speed line, even if it means limiting owners' recourse, especially farmers' [1][5].

It is a second tightening. Bill C-15, enacted on March 26, 2026, already allowed Alto to skip prior purchase negotiations and replace public hearings with written objections [5][8]. Phil Mount of the National Farmers Union is asking that no expropriation be made easier until Parliament investigates further [5].

The financial stakes are huge. On October 1, the Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated construction at C$75 billion to C$113 billion, above Ottawa's range (C$60 billion to C$90 billion), and judged an overrun more likely than savings [6][7]. The estimate assumes work starts in 2029 and a 15 km tunnel between Laval and Montreal [7].

These powers come with the 2026 budget, titled "Maîtres chez nous" (Masters in our own house), presented on November 5 by Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne. It includes C$142.1 billion in new measures [10][11].

This high-speed line has a French accent: SNCF Voyageurs and Keolis are part of the Cadence consortium, chosen in February 2025 to design, develop and operate the line. It would be the first high-speed line operated by SNCF outside Europe [9]. The battle over land will weigh on the construction timeline.

Sanctions: Brussels wants to ban the Russian flag from European stadiums and cut 60 Russian banks off from SWIFT

The European Commission has proposed the 22nd package of sanctions against Russia since 2022. It includes 60 banks cut off from the SWIFT payment system, 70 more ships from the "shadow fleet", visas denied to Russian veterans and, for the first time, a ban on the Russian flag at sports competitions in the EU [1][2][3].
The package was presented on Monday, November 23, in Brussels and detailed in the press on November 23 and 24 [1][2][5]. It will only apply if all 27 member states approve it unanimously [2][4].

Finance: 60 Russian banks would face a full transaction ban and be excluded from SWIFT, the messaging system used for international transfers [3]. The Commission is also setting up a working group on crypto-related sanctions, targeting payment networks, including platforms in third countries that help Moscow circumvent sanctions [3].

Energy and trade: 70 more ships from the "shadow fleet", the tankers that carry Russian oil despite restrictions, would be targeted [1]. Power companies would be sanctioned for the first time, and European citizens could no longer hold positions in companies in Russia [2].

Sport: teams and athletes competing under the Russian flag, as well as official Russian symbols, would be excluded from all competitions held in the EU. Russians could no longer fund sports federations based in Europe or hold positions in them [1][6].
"Sporting events cannot be a venue for propaganda," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen [3].
Visas: Russians who fought in Ukraine could no longer obtain them. This measure had been watered down in the previous package, after reluctance from Italy and France [2].
Key takeaway: after energy and finance, the EU is going after Russia's prestige. It wants to close its stadiums to the Russian flag, even as the Olympic movement reopens the door [1][5][6].

In July, the International Olympic Committee lifted the suspension of Russian athletes ahead of the Los Angeles 2028 Games, sparking an outcry in Europe. The IOC notes that visas are a matter for each state, but that athletes must not be excluded because of their nationality [6]. Moscow had warned as early as October: according to the state agency TASS, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov considers such bans contrary to Olympic ideals and to the principle of keeping sport separate from politics [7].
The banking component extends the pressure. In June, the Commission had already proposed sanctioning nearly 90 of Russia's largest banks at once [8].

Unanimity remains the main obstacle. In February 2026, Hungary and Slovakia blocked the 20th package, accusing Ukraine of disrupting their Russian oil supplies [9]. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas called it a "setback" [9].

If you go to a competition in Europe in the coming months, you may no longer see a Russian flag there, even if the IOC readmits Russian athletes. For your wallet, the effect is indirect: each package makes Russian oil and money flows a little more complicated, with no immediate effect on prices in France.

Algeria: local election campaign closes, authorities mainly fear abstention after July's record

Algeria's local election campaign ended at midnight on Tuesday, November 24. On Saturday, November 28, voters will elect their municipal and wilaya (provincial) assemblies, with a record 162,864 candidates. The real test will be turnout, which fell to about 21% in the July legislative elections [2][4][7].
The campaign, which opened on November 5, ended at midnight on Tuesday, November 24. A three-day "electoral silence" now bans all campaign activity until Friday, November 27 [2][3][8].

On Saturday, November 28, Algerians will elect, for five years, the members of the People's Municipal Assemblies (APC) and People's Wilaya Assemblies (APW), the equivalent of municipal and provincial councils, by proportional list voting [8][9].

The Independent National Electoral Authority (ANIE) counts 162,864 candidates, compared with 134,140 in 2021, and 5,995 approved lists [4][9]. It says it rejected 3 municipal lists out of 5,631 and 6 wilaya lists out of 434 [4].

According to ANIE, about 239,800 rallies and local meetings took place, in a climate it describes as "calm" [2]. Candidates mainly promised more decentralization and support for start-ups and young entrepreneurs [2].
Opposition parties, including the FFS and the RCD, protested against the exclusion of candidates from their lists [4].
The vote follows a new territorial redistricting that brings the country to 69 wilayas (provinces), which complicates the organization [10][11].
Key takeaway: President Abdelmadjid Tebboune's government does not fear defeat, but an empty room. Abstention is presented as the main issue of the vote [2].

In the July 2026 legislative elections, turnout fell to 20.79% according to ANIE's preliminary figures, then 21.24% nationwide according to the final results [6][7]. In the 2021 local elections, it reached 36.58%: that is the bar to beat [4].

Unlike in 2021, the opposition has mostly chosen to run. According to the Italian institute ISPI, a party that boycotts both the July legislative elections and the local elections now risks dissolution: taking part becomes a matter of survival more than a sign of confidence [5].

The context remains uncertain: according to the APA agency, ANIE has held many meetings and checks without dispelling doubts about the transparency of the process and political participation [8]. Saturday's results will show whether the rise in the number of candidates translates into more voters [4].

Algeria is a major neighbor of France, with strong family ties and tense diplomatic relations. Very low turnout on Saturday would be a new sign of distrust toward the authorities in Algiers, with whom Paris is struggling to restore dialogue.
